source_refs.note: Exercise 11.1, Question 6: book page 290 (Q1-Q8). The book prints no answers for Unit 11; every answer here is ours.

blocks.explanation:
Three components are given, so \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) is a 3D vector function.
We combine them with \(\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\) and state the domain.
Plan: vector form; the domain of each component (fraction, log of a root, inverse secant); their intersection.
steps:
Given: \(x(t) = \frac{1}{t+4}\), \(y(t) = \ln\sqrt{t}\), \(z(t) = \sec^{-1} t\).
To find: \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) and its domain.
Method: Step-2 and Step-3 of 11.1.3; domain \(=\) intersection of the component domains (11.2.1).

Combine into vector form
\[\mathbf{r}(t) = \dfrac{1}{t+4}\,\hat{i} + \ln\sqrt{t}\,\hat{j}\]
\[\quad + \sec^{-1}(t)\,\hat{k}\]
Since \(\ln\sqrt{t} = \ln t^{1/2} = \frac{1}{2}\ln t\), the \(\hat{j}\)-component may also be written \(\frac{1}{2}\ln t\).
Why: \(x, y, z\) go with \(\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\); the log rule \(\ln a^n = n\ln a\) (for \(a > 0\)) simplifies \(y\).

Domain of \(x(t) = \frac{1}{t+4}\)
\[t + 4 \ne 0 \Rightarrow t \ne -4\]
\[\text{domain } \mathbb{R} - \{-4\}\]
Why: division by zero is not defined.

Domain of \(y(t) = \ln\sqrt{t}\)
\(\sqrt{t}\) needs \(t \ge 0\); \(\ln\) needs \(\sqrt{t} > 0\), so
\[t > 0,\quad \text{domain } (0, \infty)\]
Why: the logarithm is defined only for positive numbers, and \(\sqrt{0} = 0\) is not positive.

Domain of \(z(t) = \sec^{-1} t\)
\[|t| \ge 1\]
\[\text{domain } (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\]
Why: \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}\) and \(|\cos\theta| \le 1\), so \(|\sec\theta| \ge 1\). Only such numbers can be values of sec, so only they have an inverse secant.

Intersection
From \(y\): \(t > 0\). Of these, \(z\) keeps only \(t \ge 1\); \(t = -4\) is already outside.
\[\text{Domain of } \mathbf{r} = [1, \infty)\]
Why: \(t\) is allowed only where all three components exist.

Check
\[\mathbf{r}(1) = \tfrac{1}{5}\,\hat{i} + 0\,\hat{j} + 0\,\hat{k}\]
exists (\(\ln 1 = 0\), \(\sec^{-1} 1 = 0\)). At \(t = \frac{1}{2}\): \(\sec^{-1}\frac{1}{2}\) is not defined, so \(t = \frac{1}{2}\) is rightly excluded \(\checkmark\).
